body:
Agricultural GIs of Gujarat

Agricultural GIs connect a crop or agricultural product with characteristics or reputation associated with a defined growing region. Gujarat's examples include fruits, wheat and dates. Unlike a craft GI, where inherited techniques may be central, agricultural GI characteristics can be closely related to local growing conditions as well as cultivation practices.

The following 4 products appear in the GI Registry's 31 December 2025 list of registered Gujarat agricultural indications.

Registered GIProductGeographical association
Gir Kesar MangoMangoGir and surrounding production region of Gujarat
Bhalia WheatWheatBhal region of Gujarat
Kachchhi KharekDatesKachchh
Amalsad ChikooChikoo, or sapotaAmalsad area of Navsari district

These associations are useful for matching questions. The legal right, however, depends on the specific geographical territory and product description in the registration, not merely on a broad district name used for revision.

Examples of registration dates

Official APEDA records identify Gir Kesar Mango and Bhalia Wheat with certificate dates of 24 June 2011. Both have Gujarat Agro Industries Corporation Limited as their registered proprietor in those records.

APEDA lists the certificate date of Kachchhi Kharek as 2 January 2024 and identifies Unidates Farmer Producer Company Limited as its registered proprietor. This illustrates how a farmer producer organisation can represent an agricultural product's interests.

In the case of Amalsad Chikoo, the GI Registry records an application filed on 16 September 2021 and registration in 2025. The filing date should not be described as the certificate date.

GIs are not limited to agriculture and handicrafts

Two Gujarat examples establish the wider scope of India's GI system:

  • Ambaji White Marble: Listed by the GI Registry under the natural goods category.
  • Surat Cut Diamond: Listed under the manufactured goods category.

A GI question may therefore be solved by identifying the kind of goods before considering the geographical association. Not every GI concerns a crop or an old textile tradition.

Registered additions identified during 2026

GI status can change as applications proceed through examination, publication and registration. Two important Gujarat developments are supported by individual GI Registry records available at the content cutoff of 14 November 2026.

Jasdan Patari Craft

Jasdan Patari Craft is associated with Jasdan in Rajkot district. The GI Registry shows application number 1194 with status Registered. Its record contains a registration certificate document dated 28 March 2026.

A Press Information Bureau release dated 15 June 2026 reported that the craft received GI recognition for 2025–26. It also identified support from the National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD) for awareness, documentation and the registration process.

Ambaji Mohanthal

Ambaji Mohanthal is a registered GI for a food product associated with Ambaji in Banaskantha district. Its official GI Registry entry records:

  • Application number: 1228.
  • Filing date: 18 April 2024.
  • Status: Registered.
  • Certificate number: 835.
  • Certificate date: 1 October 2026.
  • Registration valid up to: 17 April 2034.
  • Goods classification: Class 30, food stuffs.

The expiry date may initially appear surprising because the certificate was issued in 2026. The explanation lies in the legal rule that the registration date is treated as the application date. The 10-year period is therefore linked to the 2024 filing rather than beginning anew on the 2026 certificate date.

A GI may cover more than one state

The registered GI Warli Painting appears in the national registry as a multi-state indication that includes Gujarat alongside other territories. It should not be presented as a GI exclusive to Gujarat.

The geographical area specified in a registration is decisive. A product may be relevant to Gujarat without being registered solely for Gujarat.

Prelims focus

  • Gir Kesar Mango, Bhalia Wheat, Kachchhi Kharek and Amalsad Chikoo are registered agricultural GIs of Gujarat.
  • Ambaji White Marble is listed as a natural GI; Surat Cut Diamond as a manufactured GI.
  • Jasdan Patari Craft appears as registered in 2026 under application number 1194.
  • Ambaji Mohanthal received GI certificate number 835 on 1 October 2026.
  • Warli Painting is a multi-state GI that includes Gujarat.
  • Trap: The filing date of a GI application is not necessarily the date on which its certificate was issued.

[Sources: Geographical Indications Registry, 'State wise Registered GI of India', records as on 31 December 2025; APEDA, 'Gujarat', GI product entries for Gir Kesar Mango, Bhalia Wheat and Kachchhi Kharek; GI Registry public search, application 776, Amalsad Chikoo; application 1194, Jasdan Patari Craft; application 1228, Ambaji Mohanthal; Press Information Bureau, 'Jasdan Patari Handicraft Receives GI Recognition', 15 June 2026; Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999, sections 16 and 18; online sources consulted 14 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Mango cultivation illustrates how a recognised agricultural product can acquire a place-linked identity.

title: Gujarat's Agricultural and Other GIs: Examples and 2026 Updates

body:
How GI protection supports product branding

Buyers often cannot observe a product's full history simply by looking at it. They may not know where a textile was woven, how a craft was prepared or whether an agricultural product came from its claimed region. A GI helps communicate an established connection between goods and their geographical origin.

For this reason, effective GI branding needs more than printing a geographical name on a package. The producer must be eligible to use the registered indication, and the product must satisfy the relevant conditions of registration.

GI identity and commercial brand identity are different

A business may market genuine GI goods under its own trademark or brand. For example, an eligible Patan Patola producer may also use a distinctive business name to identify the enterprise. The 2 identifiers perform different functions.

FeatureGeographical indicationTrademark
Principal purposeIdentifies goods linked to a geographical originDistinguishes the commercial source of goods or services
Basis of identityPlace-linked quality, reputation or characteristicDistinctive sign, name, symbol or combination
Who may use itEligible registered authorised usersTrademark owner and lawful permitted users
Commercial licensingRights in a registered GI cannot be licensedTrademark rights may be licensed under applicable law

Thus, the statement that all intellectual property can be licensed is incorrect. Different forms of IP have different legal rules.

What genuine GI marketing involves

In a functioning GI market, several activities reinforce each other:

  1. Identifying eligible producers: Producers establish their connection with the defined area and the registered goods.
  2. Maintaining product characteristics: The goods follow the relevant registered description and applicable production conditions.
  3. Registering authorised users: Eligible producers obtain the statutory right to use the indication.
  4. Presenting truthful information: Labels, packaging, invoices and online descriptions identify the product without misleading buyers.
  5. Building market confidence: Producer groups, traders and consumers learn to distinguish genuine goods from imitations.

The steps are connected but distinct. Good packaging cannot replace authorised-user status, and authorised-user status does not eliminate the need for proper product handling and truthful marketing.

How misuse may occur

Suppose a seller markets an ordinary textile made outside the relevant registered geographical conditions as genuine Patan Patola. The seller may be misleading buyers about the goods' geographical origin. The use of the protected name may amount to infringement under section 22 if the statutory conditions are met.

Adding expressions such as inspired by or style does not automatically make every misleading use lawful. The actual presentation, the registered goods and the applicable legal provisions matter.

On the other hand, a trader who lawfully purchases genuine GI goods can ordinarily resell them. Section 22(4) recognises further dealings in lawfully acquired goods, including processing or packaging, except where the goods' condition is impaired after they have been put on the market. Reselling genuine goods is not the same as acquiring the right to manufacture unrelated goods under the GI.

Who can act against infringement?

Under section 21, the registered proprietor and authorised users have the right to seek relief for infringement of a registered GI. The law also addresses falsification and other prohibited uses. The GI Registry administers registration, while civil suits for GI infringement or passing off must be brought before a district court or higher court having jurisdiction.

An unregistered geographical indication does not receive the Act's statutory infringement remedy, but section 20 preserves remedies based on passing off where their requirements are established.

GI registration is not a universal quality certificate

A GI establishes a particular legally protected geographical identity. It does not, by itself, prove that every item offered for sale is genuine, safe for consumption, organically produced or compliant with every separate product standard.

Food safety requirements, grading systems and other applicable product rules remain distinct. Similarly, the presence of a geographical name or an attractive GI-style logo on packaging is not conclusive proof that the seller is an authorised user.

Economic benefits and practical limitations

GIs may help artisans and farmers distinguish their goods, reduce misleading competition and strengthen their bargaining position. To realise those benefits, producers may still require working capital, transport, marketing, packaging, cooperative organisation and links with buyers.

These needs are especially important for small producers. A registered GI provides legal protection, but commercial success depends on the product reaching buyers at a viable cost while maintaining its recognised identity.

Prelims focus

  • A GI communicates an origin-linked identity; a trademark identifies a commercial source.
  • Section 22 addresses infringement of registered GIs, including misleading indications of origin.
  • Section 20 preserves passing-off remedies even for unregistered geographical indications.
  • Section 24 prohibits commercial licensing of rights in a registered GI.
  • Lawful resale of genuine GI goods is different from manufacturing goods under a GI without entitlement.
  • Trap: GI registration is not an automatic guarantee of food safety, higher prices or universal product certification.

[Sources: Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999, sections 17 and 20–24; Intellectual Property India, 'Geographical Indications: An Introduction', sections on authorised users and infringement; WIPO, 'IP Assignment and Licensing', sections on trademarks and licensing; NCERT, Class 11, Indian Economic Development, chapter 6, 'Rural Development', section 'Agricultural Market System', printed pp. 104–106; online sources consulted 14 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: A genuine GI pathway links eligible production, registration and truthful sale; a misuse pathway shows false origin claims and possible section 22 infringement.
pictures.caption: Legal GI rights are strengthened by accurate product identification throughout the market.

title: GI Branding, Authenticity and Enforcement in Practice

body:
What is technology transfer?

Technology transfer is the movement of useful knowledge, technical capability or technology from one person or organisation to another so that it can be developed, applied or used. A university may transfer a research result to a company capable of manufacturing a product. A research institution may also share technology through collaborative research, consultancy, training or a startup.

Commercialisation is the process of turning an innovation or protected intellectual property into practical economic value, usually through the development and adoption of goods or services in a market.

The concepts overlap but are not identical. Technology transfer can occur without a commercial sale, such as through publication or research collaboration. Commercialisation generally requires a pathway to actual use and a viable market or other form of practical adoption.

Why universities work with industry

Universities are important centres of education and research. They may generate new methods, materials, products, software or technical knowledge. However, they do not always possess the factories, sales networks, capital or distribution facilities required to supply goods to large numbers of users.

Industry can contribute those capabilities. A successful collaboration allows research knowledge to reach practical users while giving companies access to useful innovation.

The main stages of commercialisation

  1. Identifying an invention: A researcher or student develops a potentially useful solution and reports it to the institution through the applicable invention-disclosure procedure.
  2. Assessing ownership and existing knowledge: The institution determines who holds the relevant rights under law, research agreements and its IP policy. It checks whether similar technology is already known.
  3. Evaluating usefulness: The invention is assessed for technical feasibility, possible applications and whether users or businesses have a need for it.
  4. Protecting suitable IP: An appropriate form of protection is considered before avoidable public disclosure, where protection is relevant.
  5. Finding a commercial partner: A company, startup or other organisation is identified to develop, manufacture or distribute the technology.
  6. Agreeing on transfer: The parties may enter a licensing, assignment, research-collaboration or another suitable agreement.
  7. Developing and supplying the product: The receiving organisation undertakes the work needed for practical market adoption.

This sequence is a common pathway rather than a compulsory order for every innovation. Some knowledge is shared openly; some technologies are commercialised through university startups; others need further development before a business is willing to adopt them.

The role of intellectual property

Different research results may call for different forms of protection:

  • Patent: Protects an eligible technical invention. In general, patentability requires novelty, an inventive step and industrial applicability, subject to legal exclusions.
  • Industrial design: Protects eligible visual features of an article, rather than the technical principle by which it works.
  • Copyright: Can protect original expression, such as qualifying written or software works, but not every idea described in them.
  • Trade secret or confidential know-how: May protect commercially valuable information kept confidential through appropriate measures and agreements.
  • Trademark: Distinguishes the commercial source of goods or services.

Not every invention must be patented. An institution may decide to publish knowledge openly, keep appropriate information confidential, or pursue another suitable approach. Protection decisions depend on the nature of the work and the applicable rights.

Licence and assignment: the central distinction

A licence permits another party to use specified intellectual property while the owner retains ownership. A licence may specify the field of use, duration, territory and payments. It may be exclusive or non-exclusive, subject to the applicable law and agreement.

An assignment transfers ownership of the relevant intellectual property rights to another party. For example, an institution might assign rights in a patent to a company, or it might retain the patent and license the company to use the invention.

Royalty refers to payment for the permitted use of intellectual property. Payments may be linked to sales, made periodically, paid as a lump sum, or structured through a combination of arrangements.

Licence: Permission to use while ownership remains with the licensor. Assignment: Transfer of ownership to the assignee.

How this differs from GI commercialisation

A Gujarat university might develop a new agricultural tool and license the relevant patented technology to a local manufacturer. That is an example of university–industry technology transfer.

By contrast, an organisation representing Patan Patola producers cannot license the registered GI right to an unrelated factory merely to collect royalties. Section 24 of the GI Act prohibits such licensing.

A GI-based craft business may still acquire and use independently licensed equipment, software or manufacturing know-how where lawful. The key distinction is that licensing technology does not transfer the separate legal right to use a geographical indication.

Prelims focus

  • Technology transfer moves knowledge or technology between organisations for development or use.
  • University–industry transfer may involve collaboration, licensing, assignment or startups.
  • A patent protects an eligible invention; a trademark identifies a commercial source.
  • Licensing permits use while ownership is retained; assignment transfers ownership.
  • Royalties are payments associated with permitted IP use.
  • Trap: Patent technology may be licensed, but rights in a registered Indian GI cannot be licensed.

[Sources: WIPO, 'FAQs: Technology Transfer', sections 'Technology transfer core concepts' and 'Technology transfer ownership issues'; WIPO, 'IP Assignment and Licensing', sections 'IP rights assignment', 'IP licensing' and 'Technology licensing agreements'; Gujarat Council on Science and Technology, 'IP Commercialisation', sections on technology assessment and licensing; Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999, section 24; online sources consulted 14 November 2026.]
